title: Gandhari sees the field
hook: the queen who chose not to see is given sight, and she sees the widows of both armies grieving the same
carry: the equal eye: their grief as your own

segments.voice: Yesterday in Stri, Gandhari held back her curse. Your line was yato dharmas tato jayah, where dharma is, victory is.

For years Gandhari has lived behind a cloth she tied on herself. Now the sage Vyasa gives her what the text calls a celestial sight, a way to see far beyond where she stands. She doesn't turn it on the sky, or the palace, or the faces of the Pandavas. She turns it on the field of Kurukshetra, where the war just ended. And beside her stands Krishna, the one person she will speak to about all of it.
screen: `A CLOTH SHE TIED HERSELF.` → `VYASA GIVES HER SIGHT.` → `SHE LOOKS AT THE FIELD.`

segments.voice: What she sees first isn't warriors. It's women. Wives, mothers and daughters of both armies move across the field, searching. Some have never walked outside the women's quarters before, and now they're out among the dead, hair loose, calling names. Gandhari describes it all to Krishna, scene after scene. She sees Uttara, the young widow of Abhimanyu, Arjuna's son, bending over him and talking to him as if he could still hear. She sees her own daughter, Duhshala, searching for her husband Jayadratha and unable to find his head. She sees her son Duryodhana on the ground, and his wife beside him. She sees Karna, and the women grieving him too. And she keeps turning to Krishna. Look at this, she says. Look at her. A Pandava widow and a Kaurava widow, doing exactly the same thing in the dust. The war books counted who killed whom. Stri counts who's left to bury them. Many teachers hear in this a teaching of the Gita: the wise look on all with an equal eye, and the highest yogi, measuring by their own heart, feels the joy and sorrow of others as their own. Hindus ground it in the Self: the same atman lives in every being, so the same grief lives in every widow. Gandhari, the Kaurava mother, doesn't stop at her own. Today, when the news counts only one side's dead, she's the one saying, look at her too.
screen: `SHE SEES THE WOMEN FIRST` · `UTTARA, DUHSHALA, DURYODHANA'S WIFE` · `GRIEF FROM BOTH CAMPS` · then, large: `THE EQUAL EYE`

segments.voice: Many Hindus end their prayers with sarve bhavantu sukhinah: may all be happy, may all be free from illness. Let your eyes rest soft, and bring to mind a conflict you know, near or far, in your family or in the news. Set aside the people who fought it, and let one person left behind on each side come into view, one with the in-breath, one with the out-breath. Then say it for both: may all be happy. If you don't pray, just hold them side by side.
Stri. Woman. The book where the women of both sides walk onto the field, and Gandhari looks at them with an equal eye.
Your line: the equal eye, their grief as your own. Tomorrow, Gandhari's grief turns on Krishna. See you then.

howItsDone: Gandhari's lament on the battlefield, spoken to Krishna, is read and retold as a passage of mourning for both sides, and many Hindus close prayers with 'sarve bhavantu sukhinah', may all be happy.
